# Statistical models in corpus linguistics {#models}

The studies in @WalkdenEa2023 rest on statistical models of a particular kind. The errors we will document are not arcane, and any reader can learn to see them. This section builds the necessary intuitions from the ground up so that by the end the reader will be able to look at the central result of the case studies and judge for themselves whether they supports anything at all.

## What a model is, and what it is for

In a corpus, we record single events of speakers/writers facing the same choice again and again. In medieval English (Section \@ref(study1)), the decision is whether to mark plural on a pre-nominal element or leave it bare.
In Spanish (Section \@ref(study2)), the decision is between expressing a pronominal subject overtly or dropping it. Each instance is a yes-or-no. We want to know which factors *push* that choice one way or the other, and how strongly they do so. Relevant factors might be the animacy of a noun's referent, the dialect region, the century. A statistical **model** is a disciplined guess at that relationship. It is a statement made by the researcher that the rate of "yes" depends on specific factors in some specified way.

The classic linguistic example is the English dative alternation (*give the book to her* versus *give her the book*). The outcome is binary (shifted or not). Candidate predictors include the animacy and length of the object [@BresnanFord2010; @WolkEa2013]. A model lets us ask how much animacy shifts the odds toward one variant, expressed as a number. That number, the **coefficient**, is usually what we are really after. As opposed to other fields, linguists are not actually invested in predicting the next sentence a speaker will produce, but rather in quantifying *what influences the choice, and by how much*. Estimating it is not a matter of belief or eyeballing. A piece of mathematics implemented in software, the **estimator**, finds the coefficient values that best fit the observed data [thorough introductions in @GelmanHill2006; @FahrmeirEa2013].

A terminological point that turns out to matter is that one does not "run a model" [@WalkdenEa2023, 558]. The researcher *specifies* a model as a complex hypothesis about what controls the variation, and the estimator then *fits* it to the data. The distinction is not pedantry. It is the difference between a causal claim one is putting to the test and a number a program happened to print.

## The original sin of destructive aggregation

Here is where the first case study (Section \@ref(study1)) goes wrong, before any model is fitted at all. The outcome is binary --- each pre-nominal element either carries plural inflection or does not. But @WalkdenEa2023 do not model those individual choices. They first *aggregate* and collapse all the instances in a text (or region, or period) into a single derived number, a difference-score, and then model *that*.

Watch what this does to a tiny sample. Suppose one text contains five relevant pre-nominal elements, of which three are inflected, and a second text contains two, of which none are.
Table \@ref(tab:simpleexample) illustrates the toy dataset.

| Text | Element | Inflection |
|------|---------|:----------:|
| A | 1 | yes |
| A | 2 | yes |
| A | 3 | no |
| A | 4 | yes |
| A | 5 | no |
| B | 1 | no |
| B | 2 | no |

: A fictitious example data set illustrating the pitfalls of aggregation {#tab:simpleexample}

Modelled directly, this is seven observations, each a genuine yes-or-no that a predictor can be tested against. Aggregated, Text A contributes the single number $0.6$ and Text B contributes $0.0$.
We end up with two data points instead of seven outcomes. And those two data points lie about the data. Text B's number, resting on two elements, carries exactly the same weight in the subsequent model estimation as A's number, aggregating five actual data points. Even a text containing five hundred elementary data points would end up contributing a single number. The within-text variation, which is the very signal we are trying to model, has been erased. The real study does this at scale and digests thousands of individual outcomes into a few dozen numbers before modelling begins. The information destroyed in that step cannot be recovered by any sophistication downstream.

## Modelling the outcome as it actually is

If we keep the data binary instead, the right tool follows naturally. We cannot use ordinary linear regression, whose predictions run off to plus and minus infinity, to model a quantity that must stay between 0 and 1 (a probability). A **Generalised Linear Model** (GLM) solves this by passing the linear combination of predictors through a *link function* that keeps predictions in range. For binary outcomes, a model with a so-called logit link and a binomial distribution is typically used (with better alternatives existing for special cases). In such models, the coefficient $\beta$ for a predictor reads as how much that predictor shifts the log-odds of "yes" [see any introduction to statistics for linguists such as @Baayen2008; @Gries2013]. The crucial gain over aggregation is that every single instance enters the model on its own terms, weighted by its own existence rather than dissolved into a group average.

One complication remains, and it is the one aggregation might be, in effect, an inadequate attempt to handle. The instances are not independent. Any number of elements from the same text (or the same author, the same region, and so on) usually shares common tendencies we have not modelled. Treating them as individual data points incorrectly pretends they are independent. A **Generalised Linear Mixed Model** (GLMM) addresses this by adding *random effects*. Random effects allow each text, speaker, and so forth to have their own baseline rates around the overall trend, so that clustered data are not mistaken for independent evidence [@Gries2015; @Schaefer2020a]. This is the standard, well-understood remedy. Aggregating the clusters away is not.

## Evaluating models

Suppose we have two fitted models and we wish to compare them, find out which one is "better" in some meaningful way. Researchers' reflex often is to reach for single-number summaries, which are not uninformative but need to be supplemented by further analyses to be interpreted competently.
Take **$R^2$**, advertised as the proportion of variance the model explains. A high $R^2$ does not guarantee a good model, and aggregation inflates it artificially: smoothing thousands of noisy binary outcomes into a few tidy averages removes exactly the variation a model is supposed to struggle with, so the model looks far more explanatory than it is. The number went up because the data were made easier, not because anything was understood.
In general, we advise to interpret only stark contrasts in $R^2$ and only for models with the same underlying distribution function and link [see @MittlboeckSchemper1996; @Tjur2009].

**Prediction accuracy** is the proportion of choices the model calls correctly. It is even more seductive and must always be read against the **base rate**, which is the accuracy reachable by blindly always guessing the most frequent outcome. If 95% of pre-nominal elements are uninflected, a model that simply predicts "uninflected" every time scores 95% while having learned nothing whatsoever. Quoted without its base rate, an accuracy figure is not evidence, it is decoration. On the other hand, a model that reaches the same 95% by actually discriminating between the cases is a different thing entirely.
However, the achievement is the discrimination, not the single number.

**Precision and recall** get at exactly that discrimination, and they split the question accuracy blurs into two. Precision is the share of correct hits among all the cases the model flags as occurrences (true positives over all predicted positives). Recall is the share of actual occurrences the model manages to catch (true positives over all real events). Crucially, the threshold that turns a probability (assigned by the model to each data point) into a yes-or-no call is not fixed at 0.5. We can slide it from 0 to 1 and track precision and recall across that range, often visualised as a pair of curves whose crossing point is a compact summary of how well the model really separates the classes. We are going to show such curves in our re-analysis of the published models later. A model that does nothing but predict the modal category lands its crossing near the base rate. A model that genuinely discriminates pushes it higher.

We have introduced the statistics tools we need for a re-analysis of the data from @WalkdenEa2023. The second case study (Section \@ref(study2)) reports, for the coefficient of its key predictor, $\beta = 0.63$ with $p = 0.049$ (Table \@ref(tab:subjectpapertable)), a result that cleared the conventional 0.05 threshold by one part in a thousand, computed on a model whose per-coefficient p-values are trustworthy only if the rest of the model is approximately right, and built on the aggregated dots we have just watched lie about the data. In the main part of this paper, we ask the relevant question: was this the output of a test with a real chance of failing? The next section answers it.
